I read "1984" yesterday and I am curious if anyone else has read it and concluded that it is a vastly overrated book. Don't get me wrong, it's a good book; it's compelling, interesting, and well written. A book can be good, though, and still be overrated and 1984 has a massive reputation.

  1. The two or three paragraphs that you see quoted everywhere are not really indicative of the whole book. They are almost taken out of context. I was expecting the novel to be more or less a blueprint for establishing a totalitarian society and that's not really it.

  2. The middle third of the book is a romance, which I enjoyed, but it doesn't add anything to the story. You could cut it completely and you don't actually miss anything. You are allowed to become invested in this relationship and then it is suddenly ended and not addressed again.

  3. The way Winston is caught is lame, to be honest. To think that he never once checked his secret room for surveillance when all it required was looking behind a painting to find a giant screen is dumb. To think he would 100% trust O'Brien on faith in an obvious trap was dumb. Winston is a smart guy and extremely paranoid and to think his undoing were two monumental blunders like that broke my immersion.

  4. I was expecting the book to be a blueprint for the totalitarian, communist future we face and I don't agree that it is. There are parallels for sure, but the system they have created and especially its motivations don't quite match. More than that, they don't make sense. The Party has created a system to give themselves power, but their power is used exclusively to maintain their power. Traditionally, power is used to live in luxury, to influence society to your liking, and/or to genocide a people. They do none of this. Their power is used to maintain this hilariously complicated system of surveillance and global war for the sake of maintaining their status and the surveillance system and war. The elite of the party don't seem to be benefiting from their power. They would have to spend all their time monitoring this system of social engineering and conflict without end.

  5. Furthermore, I think there is a failing in the theory of the elite. The Inner Party is described as a 6 million-strong "collective," but the member are specifically chosen for having the personality to be a part of the elite. I disagree that such a group of people could function as a collective. If you have selected a bunch of people solely because they are power-mad sociopaths, they won't cooperate. They will all try to gain power over each other and there will be infighting and underminding within the elite until a hierarchy is formed. Such a system could never work together in the kind of well-oiled way it would be required to maintain the totalitarian system.

  6. The ending was kind of a letdown and didn't make a lot of sense. They have this extended torture system because they believe that just killing people creates martyrs, but their system of unpersoning and vapourising people is essentially the same thing. Torturing them until they agree with you before killing them has no functional difference from just killing people except to fulfill some personal, psychopathic need to convert them. Even the way Winston is broken is underwhelming. We are supposed to believe that calling for the torture of your love in your place is the ultimate betrayal, but really, no one would be blamed considering the torture. To think that undid their entire romance was disappointing and half-arsed.

  7. Finally, the book itself is actually kind of subversive. The underlying message is that totalitarianism is bad and that democracy, egalitarianism, and liberalism are good. But democracy, egalitarianism, and liberalism are exactly why we are trending towards totalitarianism. We are getting communist governments because people vote for them and we are getting a surveillance state because we need to catch those evil bigots committing hate crimes. There is kind of a paradox in that trying to avoid 1984 by clinging to liberal values is the best way to get it.

Still a good book. I still recommend reading it with tempered expectations. I was expecting more realism, but I think it errs a little further on the side of fantasy. I think it's over-referenced. I think people who quote those same two or three paragraphs haven't actually read the book and don't understand that they are overselling it.

I believe that "1984" was published in 1949 and that is it's true value and why it is such an iconic book. The idea of outlawing love is important as love is the reason for making life worthwhile. The reason Winston gets caught is because he lets his guard down when he falls in love.
